sentences.text: Paracrax was a flightless bird with very short forelimbs and a proportionally shallow keel, similar to modern ratites.
The species possesses unique skeletal characteristics that make it easily identifiable, though these traits show vague convergence with the modern hoatzin.
Paracrax gigantea reached estimated heights of over 2 meters, making it one of the largest bathornithids and the tallest animal in its environment.
The type specimen of Paracrax antiqua was collected in Weld County, Colorado, in 1871 by Othniel Charles Marsh.
Pierce Brodkorb initially classified the remains as a turkey relative before they were correctly identified as a bathornithid.
Fossils previously thought to be a cormorant were later reidentified as remains of Paracrax antiqua.
Paracrax shared an apex predator role with large mammals like Hyaenodon, Dinictis, and Archaeotherium in its environment.
Paracrax has been synonymized with the names Meleagris antiquus and Phalacrocorax/Oligocrocorax mediterranus.
Paracrax is classified within the family Bathornithidae, though some analyses suggest it may be closer to living seriemas or outside the order Cariamiformes.

Paracrax fossils date to the Rupelian stage of the Oligocene and are found in river deposits indicating a savanna-like environment. Paracrax lived between 31.8 and 29.5 million years ago during the Rupelian stage.
Unlike its relative Bathornis which preferred wetter ecosystems, Paracrax inhabited drier environments.
It is debated whether Paracrax wetmorei was capable of limited flight, unlike its congeners.
